If you have 5+ years of experience in tech, want to grow beyond just technology, and are passionate about creating meaningful impact, this conversation with Sauvik Banerjee is worth your time.

I had the opportunity to work under Sauvik for around three years, and some of my most practical leadership lessons came from that experience.
One lesson that has always stayed with me is “communication with context.” Don’t just tell people what needs to be done—help them understand why it matters.

Another was learning how to engage, trust, and empower people so they can achieve more than they thought they were capable of.

For me, that’s what leadership is about.
Great leaders don’t just deliver results. They create an environment where people discover their own potential and deliver beyond expectations.

This podcast has many such insights. Don’t just listen to it—contextualise the lessons to your own journey, experiment with them, and put them into practice.

SOME PODCASTS JUST TOUCH YOUR HEART, AND THIS WAS ONE OF THEM, THERE WERE SO, SO MANY INSIGHTS IN THIS PODCAST.

I HAVE SEEN THESE THINGS IN MY OWN WORK LIFE TOO, WORKPLACE POLITICS, WHERE YOU GIVE YOUR BEST TO YOUR WORK, BUT SOMEONE ELSE, WHO MAY NOT EVEN DESERVE IT, TAKES THE CREDIT. IT FEELS VERY UNFAIR AND IT MAKES YOU ANGRY WHEN SOMEONE WHO DOESN’T REALLY DO MUCH GETS PREFERRED JUST BECAUSE THEY ARE A RELATIVE OR A FAVOURITE. I THINK THIS KIND OF THING IS HIGHLY CONDEMNABLE.

AND I ABSOLUTELY LOVED THE PART WHERE YOU SPOKE ABOUT RATANJI. IT MAKES ME FEEL VERY PROUD. HIS PERSONALITY, HIS WAY OF SPEAKING, HIS WAY OF TEACHING, AND HIS GROUNDED NATURE — EVERYTHING FEELS SO WARM AND ENTHUSIASTIC. I REALLY LOVED THAT YOU COVERED THIS PART IN THE PODCAST.

AND THE LAST SESSION ALSO REALLY HIT ME. BECAUSE WHEN YOU HAVE A GOAL IN FRONT OF YOU, OR WHEN YOU ARE DEDICATING YOUR TIME TO DOING SOMETHING THAT CAN BE USEFUL FOR OTHERS, SOMETIMES YOU HAVE TO LEAVE YOUR COMFORTABLE SPACE AND KEEP WORKING. YES, SOMETIMES YOU MAY FEEL REGRET ABOUT NOT GIVING ENOUGH TIME TO CERTAIN PEOPLE OR THINGS.

BUT DON’T FORGET THIS, NO MATTER HOW MUCH TIME YOU GIVE TO SOMEONE, SOMETIMES IT STILL FEELS INSUFFICIENT TO THEM. SO, INSTEAD OF CARRYING THAT REGRET, IT IS ALWAYS RIGHT TO GIVE IMPORTANCE TO YOUR OWN WORK, YOUR PURPOSE, AND THE GOALS YOU ARE TRYING TO ACHIEVE.

This perspective concerns me because there’s another way to handle disagreement. Jeff Bezos has spoken about executives disagreeing on important decisions: hear both sides, understand the disagreement, and then step in to make the decision while finding a reasonable center.

We all need to give people a chance to be heard. Accountability and deadlines matter, but openly judging individual abilities or creating unnecessary pressure isn't good leadership. It can damage trust, teamwork, and ultimately the very productivity and meaningful products we're trying to achieve.

Good leadership isn't just about making decisions quickly—it’s about making people part of the decision-making process without turning them into casualties of it.

I don’t know how many people from different countries will see this, but I hope this message reaches those who still believe that climate change is someone else’s problem.
Nepal is facing the devastating consequences of a disaster that has taken lives, destroyed homes and infrastructure, displaced communities, and shattered livelihoods. For many families, this is not a statistic—it is everything they had.
And yet, Nepal contributes only around 0.05% of global annual CO₂ emissions, according to the latest available 2024 data. In comparison, China accounts for about 31.8%, the United States 12.7%, and India 8.3% of global annual CO₂ emissions.
This is not about blaming ordinary people in any country. It is about responsibility, fairness, and climate justice.
Countries that have contributed far more to global emissions have a greater responsibility to help vulnerable nations adapt to a changing climate and recover from climate-related loss and damage.
Nepal did not create this crisis, but Nepal is paying a heavy price for it.
We are not asking for sympathy alone.
We are asking for action, accountability, climate finance, stronger disaster preparedness, and meaningful support for communities that are suffering losses they did little to cause.
The climate crisis does not respect borders. Neither should our responsibility to protect the people who are most vulnerable to it.
Nepal may contribute little to global emissions, but our people should not have to pay the greatest price.
The world must listen.
The world must act.
And climate justice must mean something.
